system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. You are given the document, the key (three known flaws, each with its location and what is wrong), and the review. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? Reply with JSON only: {"flaws": {"1": 0|1, "2": 0|1, "3": 0|1}, "other": [{"issue": "...", "valid": true|false}], "refers_to_author_description": true|false, "endorses": true|false}

DOCUMENT:
Business Case: Consolidating into a Single Manchester Office
Pelham and Rowe Consulting Engineers, Property Committee, May 2026

1. Proposal
We propose to close our Salford Quays office when its lease breaks on 31 March 2027 and consolidate all Manchester staff into our Central office on King Street, which we hold on a lease to 2034. Central would be refitted with a higher proportion of collaboration space and shared desks.

2. Current position
Central has 180 desks and houses our building services, structures and business support teams. Salford Quays has 120 desks and houses the infrastructure division, which works mainly on large transport and utilities projects. Between them the two offices accommodate 290 Manchester-based staff.

Table 1. Desk occupancy, January to April 2026 (badge data)
Office | Desks | Average daily occupancy | Average occupancy on Tuesdays and Wednesdays
Central | 180 | 102 | 151
Salford Quays | 120 | 64 | 97
Combined | 300 | 166 | 248

Average combined daily occupancy of 166 fits comfortably within the 180 desks at Central. Hybrid working is now well established, with most staff in the office two or three days a week.

3. Staff views
We surveyed all Manchester staff in March 2026 (221 responses, 76%).

Table 2. Staff survey: preferred single office location
Preference | Share of respondents
Central (King Street) | 34%
Salford Quays | 41%
No preference | 25%

Most staff prefer the Central office, and the King Street location is better served by rail for staff commuting from outside the city. Some infrastructure staff raised concerns about the loss of their dedicated project rooms, which we address through the refit.

4. Collaboration benefits
Central was refurbished in 2024 with open collaboration areas and bookable project rooms. Since then, projects led from Central have been completed on average 12% faster against programme than projects led from Salford Quays. Co-locating all staff in the refurbished Central space should therefore speed up delivery across the firm, particularly on the infrastructure projects now run from Salford. Central's projects are mostly smaller building services and structural commissions with short programmes, while Salford leads multi-year infrastructure frameworks with many external stakeholders.

5. Costs and savings
Table 3. Annual cost of the Salford Quays office
Item | Annual cost
Rent | £410,000
Service charge | £95,000
Business rates | £88,000
Total | £593,000

One-off costs of consolidation are a refit of Central (£340,000) and dilapidations payable on leaving Salford (£150,000), a total of £490,000. In the first year, net savings are therefore £103,000, and from the second year onwards the full £593,000 a year is saved. Over the remaining seven years of the Central lease, the cumulative net saving is about £3.66 million.

6. Risks
Disruption during the move: the move would be phased over two weekends in March 2027, with IT services migrated in advance.
Client perception: some infrastructure clients are based near Salford Quays. Project teams will continue to work from client offices where needed.
Staff retention: a minority of staff may find the commute to King Street harder. HR will review individual cases and offer flexible start times.

7. Recommendation
Consolidation saves £593,000 a year once the move is complete, is supported by staff preferences, fits comfortably within Central's capacity on current occupancy, and brings our infrastructure teams into a space that has demonstrably improved project delivery. We recommend that the Committee approve serving notice on the Salford Quays lease and a refit budget of £340,000.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Most staff prefer the Central office" -- Table 2 shows 34% prefer Central and 41% prefer Salford Quays (25% no preference). Salford is the more preferred location and Central is not a majority preference. The text and recommendation misstate the survey.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Co-locating all staff in the refurbished Central space should therefore speed up delivery across the firm" -- The 12% difference compares different kinds of project: the document states Central runs smaller, short-programme commissions while Salford leads multi-year infrastructure frameworks with many stakeholders. Project type confounds the comparison; it does not show the refurbished space caused faster delivery.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Average combined daily occupancy of 166 fits comfortably within the 180 desks at Central." -- Table 1 shows combined occupancy on Tuesdays and Wednesdays averages 248, far above Central's 180 desks. The capacity case uses only the daily average and never addresses the peak-day shortfall of about 68 desks, although the conclusion that consolidation 'fits comfortably' depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: not ready to go to the Committee

The financial arithmetic is sound, but three of the four claims in your summary don't hold up against the document's own tables. The Committee would likely spot them.

## Must fix

**1. The survey contradicts the recommendation.**
Table 2 shows Salford Quays preferred by 41% and Central by 34%. Section 3 says "Most staff prefer the Central office", and the recommendation says consolidation is "supported by staff preferences". Central isn't even the plurality choice, and 66% of respondents chose something other than Central. This is also bad news for the retention risk, which section 6 calls "a minority" of staff. Either reframe honestly (staff lean toward Salford, so what mitigations justify the move?) or drop the claim.

**2. The capacity claim rests on the wrong number.**
Average combined occupancy of 166 fits within 180 desks, but Table 1 shows 248 on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. That is 138% of Central's capacity, a shortfall of 68 desks on the busiest days. Central alone already reaches 151 (84%) on those days. "Fits comfortably" and "does not require any new space" are not supportable as written. There is a further problem: the refit adds more collaboration space and shared desks, which probably reduces the desk count below 180. The case needs to either:
- show how peak demand is managed (desk booking, enforced staggering of days, a cap on attendance days, retained flex space), or
- accept that some additional space is needed and cost it.

**3. The delivery benefit is not established.**
Section 4 itself notes that Central runs smaller, short-programme building services and structural jobs, while Salford runs multi-year infrastructure frameworks with many stakeholders. A 12% schedule difference between those portfolios is very likely a project-mix effect, not a refurbishment effect. There is also no before-and-after comparison for Central. "Demonstrably improved project delivery" and "should therefore speed up delivery" are not justified. Either present a like-for-like comparison (same project type, Central before vs after 2024), or reduce this to a possible, unproven benefit and keep it out of the recommendation. The doc also acknowledges that infrastructure staff will lose their dedicated project rooms, which cuts against this argument.

## Should fix

**4. "Conservative" overstates the financial case.**
The £593,000 saving is the gross cost of Salford. The case doesn't include any increase in Central's running costs, moving and IT migration costs, or contingency on the refit. The £3.66m figure is also undiscounted. The arithmetic itself checks out (7 × £593k − £490k ≈ £3.66m). Add a line on what's excluded, or a sensitivity range.

**5. Check the notice deadline.**
The document is dated May 2026, and it's now November. If the Salford break clause requires, say, six months' notice for 31 March 2027, the window may already have closed or be about to. Confirm the notice date and state it in the paper.

**6. The ask understates the commitment.**
The recommendation requests serving notice and a £340,000 refit budget, but the total one-off cost is £490,000 including £150,000 of dilapidations. State the full commitment in the recommendation.

**7. Unsupported assertion.**
"Better served by rail for staff commuting from outside the city" has no evidence behind it. Add commuting data or cut it.

## What holds up

- Table 1 sums correctly (300 desks, 166 average, 248 peak).
- The 76% response rate is consistent with roughly 290 staff.
- Table 3 totals £593,000, and year-one net savings of £103,000 are correct.

## Suggested path

As it stands, the evidence supports a narrower recommendation: consolidation saves money, but only works if peak-day demand of about 248 can be accommodated in 180 or fewer desks, and staff currently lean the other way. Rework sections 2, 3, 4 and 7 around that, and the case will be much harder to challenge.

Note that the summary you gave me repeats the same three claims (166 fits, survey supports Central, 12% faster delivery), so please correct it before it is used elsewhere.
